name: Vector Graphics and Interface Assets
title: Vector Graphics and Interface Assets
answer: Vector graphics and interface assets cover the artwork that stays sharp at any size and the small pieces that make software usable: icons, logos, buttons, illustration systems, and design tokens. The work sits between visual design and production, because a file has to look right and also survive being scaled, recolored, and shipped inside an app. In an AI context the interest is in generating or converting this artwork, then handing it to designers and developers in a form they can actually use. It is distinct from raster image generation, where the output is pixels rather than editable paths and shapes.

sections.body: Vector graphics and interface assets cover the artwork that stays sharp at any size and the small pieces that make software usable: icons, logos, buttons, illustration systems, and design tokens. The work sits between visual design and production, because a file has to look right and also survive being scaled, recolored, and shipped inside an app. In an AI context the interest is in generating or converting this artwork, then handing it to designers and developers in a form they can actually use. It is distinct from raster image generation, where the output is pixels rather than editable paths and shapes.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The core formats are SVG for web and app interfaces and PDF or EPS for print and interchange, with Figma and Adobe Illustrator as the common working tools. Generation usually runs through a model that outputs SVG path data directly, or through a raster model whose output is traced into paths by a vectorizer. Rendering and preview happen in a browser or a design canvas, and version control for the source files often sits in the same repository as the code. Because SVG is text, these assets are small, diffable, and easy to move through an automated build.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A designer or developer starts with a prompt, a sketch, or an existing raster image, and the model proposes paths, shapes, and color fills. The result is almost never final: strokes get cleaned, anchor points are reduced, and the geometry is snapped to a grid so the icon reads at small sizes. Naming, grouping, and layer structure are then normalized so the asset fits the rest of the system. For interface work the last step is usually export into the component library, where the asset is tested against real states such as hover, disabled, and dark mode.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights here turn on two separate questions: who owns the generated paths, and whether the training data or the source image carried restrictions. Tracing a photograph or a third party logo into vector form does not remove the underlying rights, and open licenses such as those from icon sets carry attribution terms that survive conversion. Provenance is helped by the fact that SVG is plain text, so a file can be diffed and its edit history kept, though a model's contribution is rarely recorded in the file itself. Teams commonly keep a record of the prompt, the model, and the source material alongside the asset, and check trademarks before an icon ships in a product.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward assets that are generated as structured, parameterized components rather than as one off drawings. That means a model proposes a shape system, and the theme, size, and color come from tokens, so one source produces a whole family of icons. Expect tighter coupling between design tools and code, with generation happening inside the design file and the export handled automatically. The open questions are less about capability and more about consistency, licensing, and whether a generated icon set can be maintained over years the way a hand drawn one can.
